title: Eval sweep: batching + caching + max_tokens — latency / cost / quality notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc records the applied-ML onboarding experiments we ran to quantify the latency / cost / quality tradeoffs when varying three operational levers: batching, prefix/KV caching, and max_tokens. Goal is a practical decision matrix for which model variants and serving configs we recommend for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private early rollouts.

Context / motivation:
- New model family X-3.1 has strong offline quality but unknown runtime characteristics for typical Redwood workloads (interactive chat + short completion + embeddings-driven rerank).
- Product asks: can we squeeze cost without materially harming quality? Primary levers: increase batch size to improve GPU utilization, enable prefix/KV caching for repeated conversation contexts, and reduce max_tokens for bounded replies.
- This is a working notes doc; contains raw observations, oddities, and steps to reproduce.

Experimental design (high level):
- Workloads tested:
  1) Chat short: median prompt 28 tokens, target response median 40 tokens. (User-facing assistant)
  2) Long completion: median prompt 120 tokens, target response median 512 tokens. (SaaS-copy generation)
  3) Rerank/embedding pattern: many short prompts batched for embedding generation and reranking.
- Model variant: X-3.1 FP16 (baseline), X-3.1 int8 (quantized experimental).
- Hardware: p4d-like instance (A100 equiv) and small T4-like instance (for Dedicated low-cost tier).
- Sweep parameters:
  - Batch sizes: [1, 4, 8, 16, 32] (for generation), [1, 16, 64, 256] for embeddings
  - Caching: [off, prefix_cache_enabled] (KV cache warm/cold scenarios were measured separately)
  - max_tokens (generation cap): [64, 128, 256, 512]
  - Concurrent clients: [1, 8, 32] to simulate QPS pressure and batching dynamics.
- Metrics collected per run: p50/p95 latency (ms), tokens/sec, GPU utilization (%), per-1M-token estimated infra cost (USD), quality metrics: BLEU/ROUGE for generation datasets, embedding cosine avg. similarity for semantic tasks, and a small human preference sample (n=120) for chat quality.

Prompt sets / evals used:
- chat-short-prompts-2025-11: 500 prompts sampled from product chat logs (anonymized).
- long-gen-contrast-2025: 200 seed prompts used for content generation evals (diverse domains).
- rerank-sim-2025: 1k short queries paired with candidate docs; offline MRR and embedding-sim used.
- Hand-labeled subset (human-eval-chat-120) used for pairwise preference testing across configuration pairs.

Key observations (summary):
1) Batching gains are real but taper quickly for interactive chat: going from batch=1 to batch=8 reduces p50 by ~20% on A100-equivalent; further increases to 16/32 increase throughput but add queuing/variance, hurting p95 latency. For user-facing chat, batch=4 is a sweet spot on heavy-hardware.

2) Caching (prefix/KV) drastically reduces cost for multi-turn flows where prefixes repeat: in our warm-cache experiments, per-token GPU compute dropped ~35% and p50 latency of subsequent messages dropped ~40%. Cold-cache first request still incurs full compute so tail p95 is unchanged unless we pre-warm.

3) max_tokens cap reduces both latency and cost linearly with average tokens generated, but quality degradation depends on workload: chat-short tolerates cap=64 with minimal human-eval delta (preference change < 4%), while long completions drop coherence and BLEU/ROUGE by 8–18% when capped at 256 vs 512.

4) Quantized int8 variant reduces per-token cost estimate by ~22% with small (1–3%) quality regression on embedding similarity, but increases variance in long generation (occasional hallucination cases flagged in human eval sample). Recommend careful A/B gating for int8 on critical workloads.

5) Under higher concurrency (32 concurrent clients), batching effects are more pronounced and can yield >2x throughput improvements on Dedicated, but p95 latency for chat suffers unless we enforce a latency-aware routing policy (limit batch windows).

Representative numbers (rounded):
- Chat short, A100, FP16, batch=1, cache=off, max_tokens=128: p50=85ms, p95=310ms, tokens/sec=120, est cost/1M tokens=~$210. Human pref baseline.
- Chat short, A100, FP16, batch=4, cache=off, max_tokens=128: p50=68ms, p95=420ms, tokens/sec=210, est cost/1M tokens=~$135. Slightly worse p95 due to queuing, but p50 improved.
- Chat short, A100, FP16, batch=4, cache=on (warm), max_tokens=128: p50=38ms, p95=170ms, tokens/sec=350, est cost/1M tokens=~$85. Human pref delta: -2%.
- Long gen, A100, FP16, batch=1, cache=off, max_tokens=512: p50=420ms, p95=1.8s, tokens/sec=9, est cost/1M tokens=~$1200.
- Long gen, A100, int8, batch=4, cache=off, max_tokens=256: p50=330ms, p95=2.1s, tokens/sec=11, est cost/1M tokens=~$930. Quality BLEU drop ~10% vs FP16 512.
- Embeddings, T4-like, batch=256, cache=N/A, est throughput 12k/sec, cost/1M vectors ~$45 (quantized model gave 30% savings).

Notes on measurement caveats and anomalies:
- p95 sometimes worse at mid batch sizes (4–16) than batch=32. Root cause: scheduling jitter + uneven request arrival patterns in our synthetic driver. Real traffic with bursty user behavior will push more queuing.
- Warm-cache numbers assume a realistic TTL and reuse rate; we measured warm caches with 60% prefix reuse. If reuse <20%, benefits drop sharply.
- Int8 variant produced a small number (4/120) of clearly incoherent completions in human eval for long-gen; need targeted tests on hallucination risk before enabling for customer-facing long-text features.

Decision matrix / practical recommendations (first pass):
- Hosted API (default):
  * Chat-short: enable prefix caching by default, batch window short (<=10ms) but allow batch=4 where hardware supports. Default max_tokens=128. Use FP16 as default; offer int8 as opt-in with explicit warning and higher QA gating.
  * Long-gen: keep batch=1 or low (<=4), keep FP16 by default, default max_tokens=512. For cost-savvy customers, offer quantized variants behind a flag with best-effort A/B monitoring.
  * Embeddings/rerank: large batch sizes (>=256) on Dedicated pools or separate embeddings clusters; promote int8 quantized embedding model aggressively for cost.

- Dedicated: allow customers to pick throughput-optimized profiles (batch up to 32) but expose latency SLO tradeoff. Provide a "low-latency" config (batch <=4, cache enabled) and "throughput-first" config (higher batch, pre-warm strategies).

- Private: surface the same knobs in Console with recommended presets and a simple cost estimator. Encourage customers to run a short automated workload replay to calibrate cache reuse and batch sizing.

Operational/implementation notes for Console and Runtime teams:
- Add a simple slider in Console for "batch aggressiveness" and preview of expected p50/p95 and cost delta (based on these results).
- Expose a cache pre-warm API for customers that want low p95 for cold-start flows (e.g., onboarding demos).
- Integrate model-quality regression checks: when enabling int8 or lower max_tokens defaults, automatically run the paired eval prompt-set and a small human-A/B or proxy metric (embedding-sim) before rollout.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How stable are these numbers on other hardware (V100, lower-end GA4)? Need a short cross-hardware sweep.
- For chat, what is realistic prefix reuse rate across customers? We used conservative 60% for some consumer apps but only 20–30% observed in enterprise support chats — we should segment reuse by product.
- Should we instrument per-route cache reuse in the runtime to automatically recommend pre-warm policies?
- Need a larger human-eval sample for int8 long-gen to estimate hallucination frequency with tighter confidence intervals (target n=500).

Repro steps (short):
1) Checkout eval-harness branch sweep-batch-cache-2026.
2) Run driver with flags: --model X-3.1 --quant int8|fp16 --batch [1,4,8] --cache [on|off] --max-tokens [64|128|256|512] --concurrency [1|8|32] --workload [chat-short|long-gen|embeddings].
3) Upload raw CSVs to gs://redwood-internal/evals/<run-id>. Use run-id in linked_artifacts.

Appendix: quick heuristics for product teams (one-liners)
- If <200ms p50 is a hard rule for your UX, keep batch <=4 and use warm caches or smaller max_tokens.
- If cost per 1M tokens is dominant for your pricing model, prioritize embedding quantization and batching aggressively; accept wider p95 and add fallback policies.
- For new model onboards: always run the small human-eval (n>=120) on any quantized variant before enabling for default routes.
